claim: When a Bevel (edge or modifier) crosses a convex corner and produces bad/pinched shading, check the Bevel's corner/miter setting -- switching it from the default to 'Arc' specifically resolves shading problems at convex corners under Subdivision Surface. This is described as a required fix step, not an optional tweak.
supporting_evidence: Direct quote (~12:55): "it's really important to look into convex Corners like this and make sure that this is actually a little bit different... now before you do anything we need to change these Corners because they're going to cause a lot of problems so go to Bevel settings and simply change to Arc this is what you want"
rejected_alternative: Leaving the Bevel's corner/miter type at its default setting on a convex corner
reason: The default corner type was observed to cause shading problems specifically at convex corners; Arc was chosen to fix it.

claim: The Bevel tool/modifier's 'Surface Slide' option makes the bevel geometry slide along the underlying surface's curvature instead of projecting in a flat/linear way -- useful specifically on curved corners where a straight bevel produces worse shading than one that follows the curve.
supporting_evidence: Direct quote (~12:38): "we could turn on the um surface slide in here and I think I wonder if this would work actually let's go with surface slide and I think this is going to be a little better because it's going to slide on the curvature here and it's going to produce a better shading"

claim: An alternative fix for SubD pinching at a corner/loop besides re-routing topology with the knife tool: grab the entire loop causing the pinch and drop/move it to stretch and relax that region of the mesh, removing a redundant edge and reforming the area into a clean quad -- a direct manual reshaping fix rather than a topology-redirect operation.
supporting_evidence: Direct quote (~14:16): "if the shading is pinched like here what we can do is we can actually remove this one and sort of stretch this okay so grab this entire Loop and drop it down and this will stretch and relax this entire area here and then remove this one and create a quad and this should be much better"
rejected_alternative: Re-routing the pinched area with the knife tool (the topology-redirect technique)

claim: Triangles and n-gons are acceptable and don't need to be forcibly eliminated when they sit on a genuinely flat surface, or even on a non-flat area if the actual subdivided shading result still comes out clean -- the deciding test is the rendered/subdivided shading result, not a blanket rule against non-quads.
supporting_evidence: Direct quotes: "you could leave this quad here just on the triangle triangles are fine guys you know as as long as you you know know what you're doing" (~16:37); and later, pointing at an n-gon that still shades cleanly: "this is an ngon which is funny because it's shading perfectly you see sometimes ngon cause zero problems now this one is on the flat surface so this is why it works... but you know if you really wanted to fix this we could... but this angle doesn't really do any hard harm so you can leave it you know so sometimes even end guns are fine" (~21:21)
rejected_alternative: Always eliminating every triangle/n-gon regardless of whether it visibly affects shading
reason: Forcing every polygon to be a quad is unnecessary work when the actual shaded result already reads cleanly, particularly on flat surfaces where curvature-related distortion isn't a risk.
